Accents on a Non-Final Atom of a Compound

Maqaf marks join two or more atoms into a single chanted word. In the prose system a chanted word usually has exactly one accent. In a small minority of cases, a chanted word has two accents, but never more than two. Of the 36,786 maqaf compounds in the prose verses of MAM, 233 (0.63%) have an accent on a non-final atom. In every one of them the two accents sit on two atoms of the compound and never both on one, the compound itself having two atoms, or occasionally three. This page counts those cases, sorts them, and asks what they mean for the chanted word

ל֣א־תעש֣ה

in Koren's Deuteronomy appendix Decalogue (the p-trad עליון) — a maqaf compound with a munaḥ on both of its atoms. The Wikisource strand Koren otherwise follows in every accent has

ל֣א תעש֣ה

instead: two chanted words, each with a munaḥ of its own.

The odd maqaf in Koren might simply be accidentally carried over from the p-trad תחתון:

לא־תעש֨ה

Koren's is not the only such compound in print. The Simanim Tiqqun has a munaḥ on the joined לא of two compounds, where its Wikisource strand, the Exodus p-trad תחתון, has a meteg:

ל֣א־יהי֥ה

ל֣א־תעש֨ה

The second accent is a merkha in the first of those and a qadma in the second, so neither is Koren's munaḥ twice; but each of the three is one maqaf compound with an accent on both of its atoms.

But if we take these maqafs seriously, is there anything in Tanakh like any of the three?

There is not. No maqaf compound in MAM's prose verses has the same accent on both atoms, not once, which disposes of Koren's; and the Simanim Tiqqun's two pairs, a munaḥ before a merkha and a munaḥ before a qadma, occur on no chanted word of those verses at all, compound or simple. Of the 233 prose cases, 211 are a single grammatical category, metigah-zaqef: a qadma before a zaqef.

The prose verses

Two accents can appear on a chanted word, whether it is compound or simple. These are the pairs that occur on a compound, in the prose verses of MAM, with an example of each and how often each occurs on a simple chanted word as well:

Most of these pairs are covered in Yeivin's ITM §§210, 216, 221, 224, 233 and 241.

MAM catalogues two of these accents place by place, in its features-of-interest lists: every merkha of this kind and every mahapakh.

The poetic verses

The poetic system is a different matter, and different enough that the same count would not mean the same thing there. It puts two marks on one chanted word readily and systematically (Breuer, CoS ch. 9 §§20–26), where the prose system does so rarely, and in the few pairs above. And many of its maqafs are not written at all: Breuer (§§27, 37) records that in poetic verses the maqaf after a secondary mark is customarily left unwritten while the atom still counts as joined, so a survey that finds compounds by looking for a written maqaf reaches only part of what is there. MAM's poetic verses have 17 cases by that measure, and MAM has the other part of the measure too: it supplies 116 gray maqafs, its mark for a maqaf the manuscript leaves unwritten where the chanted word needs one. Of those, 69 join an atom that has an accent alongside the compound's accent; the other 47 have one accent written across the two atoms. Neither figure belongs beside the prose one.

One row is written ger./az. because its second accent goes by two names: in some traditions a geresh on a chanted word stressed on its last syllable is called an azla (Jacobson, CHB p. 187). Which name each of the 99 takes turns on that stress, which this table does not record.

The simple counts on this page leave out six chanted words that have two accents graphically, but whose two accents likely belong to one syllable. They are listed in an appendix below.

Appendix: the chanted words whose two marks sit on one letter

These six chanted words are in none of the tables above. Each has its two accents on one letter, so it is not clear that the two belong to different syllables. MAM's features-of-interest lists have the five with a telisha gedolah among them. Two of them have each of their two marks written twice, so they look at first like four accents rather than two; MAM treats the later pair as a stress helper. The Mwd column links each chanted word to MAM's notes on it.
